title: Why You Refuse to Kill Flawed Projects You Built Yourself
alt_title_1: The IKEA Effect: How Personal Effort Blinds Smart Builders
alt_title_2: Dan Ariely's 2012 Study on Overvaluing Your Own Creations
description_hook: In 2012, behavioral scientists Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon, and Dan Ariely showed that assembling something yourself inflates its perceived value by up to 63%. Here is how builders use the Outsider Replacement Test to beat the IKEA Effect.

affiliate_cta.offer_name: Project Kill-Criteria Matrix + Behavioral Strategy Reading List
affiliate_cta.pinned_comment: What is one complex workflow or side project you kept alive too long simply because you built it yourself? 👇 Grab our Project Kill-Criteria Matrix + reading list here: https://kenvh0010-lang.github.io/admin/bio/

scenes.headline: Why DIY Effort Blinds Objective Judgment
scenes.stat_label: EXTRA VALUE ASSIGNED TO SELF-BUILT ITEMS
bullets: Purchased tools are easy to cancel when they underperform
Self-built systems trigger emotional attachment and defense
scenes.narration: The hardest project to shut down is never the expensive tool you bought; it is the clunky system you built with your own hands.
scenes.source: Norton, Mochon & Ariely, Journal of Consumer Psychology (2012)

scenes.headline: Norton, Mochon & Ariely's 2012 Origami Test
scenes.stat_label: WHEN LABOR LEADS TO IRRATIONAL PRIDE
bullets: Subjects folded clumsy origami and built plain storage boxes
Builders priced their own boxes 63% above pre-built ones
scenes.narration: In 2012, researchers Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon, and Dan Ariely demonstrated the IKEA Effect in the Journal of Consumer Psychology. Participants who assembled plain boxes and paper origami valued their amateur creations up to sixty-three percent higher.
scenes.source: Norton, Mochon & Ariely, 'The IKEA Effect: When Labor Leads to Love', JCP (2012)

scenes.headline: Confusing Personal Sweat With Market Demand
scenes.left_body: Months of custom code or slides -> kept alive despite zero buyers
scenes.right_body: Judged strictly on user results -> prune dead weight fast
scenes.narration: Sweat distorts judgment. Founders and engineers pour months into lukewarm products or tangled spreadsheets because personal labor masquerades as market value.

scenes.headline: Run the Outsider Replacement Test Quarterly
scenes.stat_subtext: Cut low-traction DIY projects -> double down on proven winners
scenes.narration: Protect your hours with the Outsider Replacement Test: ask whether an objective stranger taking your seat today would pay for or rebuild this project from scratch.
scenes.source: Inspired by Andy Grove's replacement test, Only the Paranoid Survive (1996)

scenes.headline: Price Outcomes, Never Effort
scenes.stat_label: CUSTOMERS PAY FOR UTILITY, NOT YOUR HOURS
bullets: Retire unloved features quickly to reclaim creative energy
Keep the lesson learned and let go of the artifact
scenes.narration: Judge your work by the problem it solves for others, never by the hours it cost you.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule of thumb (advice, not a study)
